newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thai bourse battered, Hong Kong's close a record.
newsitem.headline: Thai bourse battered, Hong Kong's close a record.

text.p: Investors baled out of Thai stocks on Monday following the weekend general election, slashing almost six percent off the Bangkok bourse.

The New Aspiration Party's (NAP) election victory sent the SET index plummeting 5.83 percent, ending 58.39 points lower at 942.34 amid anxiety over a new coalition government and its economic team, brokers said.
In other Asian markets, Hong Kong's key Hang Seng index added 1.19 percent to notch a record high close but Tokyo's Nikkei lost half a percent.
Bangkok's plunge reversed a two-week rally that had been building in anticipation of a victory for the NAP's archrival, the Democrat Party, led by former premier Chuan Leekpai.
"Investors are disappointed that the Democrat Party did not win the election and form the new government," said one analyst at United Securities.

Before the election, investors had pinned their hopes on a win by the Democrats because the party was seen as having a strong economic team that could bolster Thailand's slowing economy, brokers said.

The NAP, led by Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, announced that it was forming a coalition with five other parties which mostly belonged to the troubled departing administration of premier Banharn Silpa-archa. Chavalit is set to be the next premier.
Brokers in Hong Kong said optimism about the property sector drove property stocks sharply higher, boosting the overall tone.
The Hang Seng closed on a gain of 153.43 points at 13,042.80 after reaching an all-time intra-day high at 13,094.42.
Antony Mak, sales director at Vickers Ballas, said investors considered Friday's 115.43-point Hang Seng drop as a buying opportunity. "People are buying on every dip," he said.
"Property is again under the spotlight because property prices recently continued to move up," said Mak.
Tokyo stocks closed weaker on an unclear outlook over Japan's financial reform plans and its economic recovery, brokers said. Volume was the year's smallest.
The key Nikkei 225 average was down 133.36 points or 0.64 percent at 20,796.37.
"The only thing we can say about the market is that we don't have anything to trade on," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last week unveiled a five-year plan to liberalise financial markets by 2001.
Taiwan share prices finished at a 1996 high as a bank's projection of soaring profits for giant Formosa Plastics group fuelled wider buying, brokers said.
The weighted index ended 63.62 points or 0.96 percent higher at 6,659.72.
The previous year high was on November 6 when the index finished at 6653.65.
A Mitsubishi Bank report said Formosa Plastics group's multi-billion-dollar petrochemical project, to open in 1999, would boost the conglomerate into one of the island's best long-term investments.
The Philippine share index closed up by 32.76 points, or 1.07 percent, at 3,105.55 points on the forthcoming APEC summit and release of gross national product (GNP) data, traders said.
Singapore shares slipped, the Straits Times Industrials Index closing down 15.61 points or 0.71 percent at 2,178.03.
At 1105 GMT, the dollar traded at 111.38/1.43 yen and 1.5058/61 marks.
Hong Kong gold prices ended a shade down at $380.00/50 an ounce against Friday's New York close of $380.05/55.
SIMEX Brent crude futures fell. The January contract last traded at $23.19 per barrel, down 11 cents from London's Friday close.
